summary: Defines the Aggregation MIB modules, used to configure a management agent to combine the values of a chosen set of managed objects and answer queries about them. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A tool that gathers lots of numbers from a machine into one summary sheet so you can ask once instead of many times.

subtitle: Combining network management data into single objects to reduce traffic.

tldr.problem: Network management requires polling many individual objects, which sends many query packets over the network and consumes bandwidth for redundant object identifiers in every request and response.
tldr.mechanism: The Aggregation MIB lets a manager define an Aggregate Managed Object that bundles multiple target objects, then query one aggregate object instead of many individual ones. A variant supports time-based aggregation of repeated samples of a single object.
tldr.outcome: Managers can reduce the number of management queries and the bandwidth they consume, though the RFC notes care is needed to avoid response sizes exceeding message limits.

today: RFC 4498 is Experimental. It provides a standardized way for SNMP managers to reduce network management traffic by aggregating multiple managed objects into single queries, though alternative approaches to reducing management traffic exist.

sections.title: Management Information Aggregation
sections.content:
Network management relies on querying managed objects (MOs) via SNMP, but each query carries overhead. The cost includes network bandwidth, packet processing at both manager and agent, and the repetition of object identifiers in requests and responses. When a manager needs to poll hundreds of individual managed objects, these costs accumulate.

This RFC proposes two complementary approaches to reduce this overhead. The basic Aggregation MIB allows a manager to combine multiple independent managed object instances into a single Aggregate Managed Object (AgMO), bundling their values into one response. A second approach, Time-Based Aggregation (TAgMO), bundles multiple samples of the same object taken at regular intervals into a single aggregated value.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine asking your friend for their height, weight, and age in three separate questions. Instead, you could ask for all three at once and get back one answer with all the numbers together.

sections.title: Aggregation Concepts
sections.content:
An Aggregate Managed Object is defined by specifying a list of source managed object instances in order. When queried, the agent concatenates the values of all source objects and returns them as a single OCTET STRING. The manager application must know the source objects and their order to interpret the response correctly. Each aggregate object is accompanied by an ErrorStatus object that reports any errors encountered while fetching the constituent objects, with the error paired to the position of the failed object.

Time-Based Aggregation extends this concept by sampling a single managed object at regular intervals. The manager specifies the sampling interval, the number of samples desired, and the target object. The aggregate value includes a timestamp (the sysUpTime when the first sample was taken) followed by the sampled values. This allows a manager to collect a series of values without issuing multiple queries.
sections.plainLanguage: With regular aggregation, you ask for the values of different numbers all at once. With time-based aggregation, you ask for the same number checked at different times all bundled together.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Tables
sections.content:
The Aggregation MIB consists of two separate modules. The AggrMIB defines regular aggregation through three tables: the aggrCtlTable (control), the aggrMOTable (definitions of constituent objects), and the aggrDataTable (the aggregated values and error information). Each row in aggrCtlTable defines one aggregate object by ID and specifies its control parameters including a compression algorithm and storage type.

The TAggrMIB for time-based aggregation has a simpler structure with just two tables: the tAggrCtlTable and tAggrDataTable. Rows in tAggrCtlTable define which object to sample, at what interval, and how many samples to collect. Both MIB modules support optional compression of aggregated data using the DEFLATE algorithm (RFC 1951, used in gzip), allowing agents and managers to trade CPU for bandwidth reduction.
sections.plainLanguage: The SNMP module defines tables that let you set up which objects to combine and how to combine them, similar to setting up a spreadsheet formula to add up cells.

sections.title: Configuration and Usage
sections.content:
A manager must know the specific managed object instances to aggregate before configuring an aggregate object. If a manager does not know the target object instances, it must first discover them by walking the MIB tree on the agent. The RFC recommends this discovery only when the resulting aggregation will be used repeatedly, so the benefits outweigh the cost of the initial discovery walk.

When configuring aggregation, managers must be careful not to create responses larger than the maximum SNMP message size. If an aggregated value exceeds the size limit, the agent returns a tooBig error. Entries in the control tables can be configured with owner identification and storage type (volatile or permanent) to control their lifecycle across agent reboots.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to know what numbers you want to combine before you set it up. You also need to make sure the combined answer is not so big that the network chokes on it.

sections.title: Compression and Performance
sections.content:
The Aggregation MIB defines a compression algorithm field that supports no compression (default) or the DEFLATE algorithm. Compression is optional at the implementation level but, when used, significantly reduces the size of aggregate values. This is particularly valuable for time-based aggregation where many samples can create large payloads.

The RFC acknowledges that bandwidth savings depend on how frequently aggregation is used and how many constituent objects are in each aggregate. Applications that poll the same aggregate repeatedly, or that bundle large time-series data, see the greatest benefit. The RFC notes that SNMP agents are expected to perform the aggregation work, reducing the number of individual object lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the machine to pack the numbers tightly (like with a zip file) so they take less space when traveling over the network, or leave them unpacked if you prefer simplicity.
